Mifamurtide after osteosarcoma surgeryNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00100

One infusion per page. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
These are reusable treatment records; their number does not define the course length. Ask for additional sheets as needed.

Mifamurtide stimulates innate immune cells to help act against remaining osteosarcoma cells after complete surgery. It is an additional postoperative treatment discussed with the patient and family, alongside chemotherapy.

Mifamurtide resembles part of a bacterial cell wall and stimulates monocytes and macrophages, cells of the innate immune system. The aim is to help these cells act against remaining osteosarcoma cells after complete surgery. It accompanies postoperative chemotherapy. It is not an immune checkpoint inhibitor.

Chemotherapy treats osteosarcoma cells throughout the body, including cells too small to see on scans, alongside surgery intended to remove the visible cancer.

Doxorubicin enters deoxyribonucleic acid, the genetic material called deoxyribonucleic acid (the cell’s genetic material) (DNA), and interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme needed when cells copy and repair their genes. This damages tumour cells. Normal marrow, mouth and heart cells can also be injured.
What to watch forReport fever, mouth ulcers, breathlessness, ankle swelling, palpitations or pain at the drip immediately.

Cisplatin forms links within and between strands of DNA, the genetic material. These links stop cells copying their instructions normally. Kidney cells, the inner ear and nerves may also be injured, so prescribed fluids and organ checks are essential.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, ringing ears, hearing changes, numbness or weakness before further treatment.

The three medicines act through different mechanisms against osteosarcoma throughout the body. Surgery removes the visible tumour, and chemotherapy before and after surgery aims to reduce recurrence risk.

Methotrexate blocks processes that use folate to make deoxyribonucleic acid (the cell’s genetic material) (DNA), the genetic material. At this high dose it requires carefully timed folinic acid rescue to protect healthy cells. The kidneys remove methotrexate: slow removal can increase exposure and severe toxicity. Hydration, urine alkalinisation, blood levels and rescue are inseparable parts of treatment.
What to watch forReport mouth ulcers, severe diarrhoea, reduced urine, dry cough, breathlessness or new neurological symptoms urgently. Do not stop rescue medicine or start other medicines yourself.

Doxorubicin enters deoxyribonucleic acid, the genetic material called DNA, and interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme needed when cells copy and repair their genes. This damages tumour cells. Normal marrow, mouth and heart cells can also be injured.
What to watch forReport fever, mouth ulcers, breathlessness, ankle swelling, palpitations or pain at the drip immediately.

Cisplatin forms links within and between strands of DNA, the genetic material. These links stop cells copying their instructions normally. Kidney cells, the inner ear and nerves may also be injured, so prescribed fluids and organ checks are essential.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, ringing ears, hearing changes, numbness or weakness before further treatment.

The two medicines damage tumour genetic material through different mechanisms to help control sarcoma. The intended role, chance of benefit and how this fits with surgery, radiotherapy or trials depend on the diagnosis and previous treatment.

The liver converts ifosfamide into active compounds that crosslink deoxyribonucleic acid (the cell’s genetic material) (DNA), the genetic material, preventing normal cell division. Other breakdown products can damage the bladder, kidneys or brain. Mesna reduces bladder injury; it does not prevent kidney injury or brain toxicity.
What to watch forNew confusion, unusual sleepiness, hallucinations, unsteadiness, seizures, blood in urine or reduced urine needs immediate assessment.

Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that controls breaks in DNA, the genetic material. Damaged tumour cells cannot divide normally. The bone marrow and other healthy tissues are also affected.
What to watch forTell the nurse immediately about dizziness, flushing, rash, chest tightness, breathlessness or feeling faint during infusion.
